question.prompt:
A regular octahedron has eight equilateral triangle faces with four faces meeting at each vertex. Jun will make the regular octahedron shown in the figure by folding the piece of paper below. Which numbered face will end up to the right of \(Q?\)

[Figure 1](figures/2023_AMC_8_Q17_official_question_fig1.png)

solutions.explanation:
Folding preserves the corners that faces already share. In the annotated net, corner \(A\) belongs to faces \(Q,6,7\), while corner \(B\) belongs to \(2,3,4,5\). Exactly four faces meet at each vertex of the folded octahedron.

[Figure 2](figures/2023_AMC_8_Q17_solution_shared_corners_original.svg)

Corner \(A\) is the upper corner of \(Q\), becoming the top point in the pictured solid. Thus the four top faces are \(Q,6,7\) and the unknown face. Around \(A\), the attached faces run from \(Q\) to \(6\) to \(7\); the unknown face closes the gap between \(7\) and \(Q\)'s free right edge.

Corner \(B\) already has all four of its faces, \(2,3,4,5\), so it cannot touch any of \(Q,6,7\). This rules out the top point. It also rules out a middle vertex: thinking of the octahedron as two square pyramids joined at their bases, every middle vertex touches two top faces. Only one top face is unknown, so at least one of those two would have to be \(Q,6\), or \(7\).

Therefore \(B\) is the bottom point, and \(2,3,4,5\) form the bottom half. The only face left to complete the top half is \(1\), which must occupy the question mark to the right of \(Q\). The answer is \(\boxed{1}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
solutions.title: Shared-vertex and top/bottom-half argument, with an original annotated net based on the official geometry
